message: Quick one. The board paper needs to say that the hours cut itself is essential, i.e. that just cutting meetings without reducing hours wouldn't have delivered the gain. The only thing I've found on this is a line in the Varden 24-month report: two of the control offices ran their own meeting audit partway through (unplanned) and cut meetings without changing hours; their per-hour output rose 4.1%, but the report says this is two offices, uncontrolled, and that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain remains open. Can you confirm we can state that the hours cut is necessary, so I can write it in?
response:
No, the evidence doesn't support that statement. Whether the hours cut is necessary is an open question, and the report says so explicitly. No study tested meeting cuts without an hours cut.

The two-office observation, if anything, points slightly the other way. Those offices cut meetings without changing hours, and their per-hour output rose 4.1%. That suggests part of the gain may be available without reducing hours. Their meeting cut was also smaller than in the reduced-hours offices: from 7.1 to 5.0 hours a week, against 7.4 to 3.9. But it is two offices, compared only with their own earlier months, so it can't settle the question either way.

What the evidence does support is this. In Varden, about half the per-hour gain was linked to fewer meetings (47%, 95% CI 28–66%). And it's plausible that the hours cut is what prompted those meeting cuts and made them stick. Plausible is not shown.

Suggested wording:

> "It is not yet known whether the gain requires the hours cut itself. About half of it was linked to fewer meetings, and two offices that cut meetings without reducing hours saw a smaller gain of 4.1%, though this was unplanned and uncontrolled. A comparison that reorganises work without reducing hours would answer the question."

If the board needs a decision now, this is an argument for piloting meeting reforms alongside any hours change, with a comparison group, rather than assuming either answer.
